rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the four-sūrah sequence, al-An‘ām conclusively presents truth to Quraysh, while al-A‘rāf warns them.
rows.anchor: Sūrah al-An‘ām conclusively communicates the truth to the Quraysh. Sūrah al-A‘rāf sounds a warning to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Anfāl prepares believers for jihād and announces Quraysh's removal from custodianship of the House of God.
rows.anchor: the divine decision is taken to depose the Quraysh from the custodianship of the House of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tawbah issues Quraysh an ultimatum and gives the Hypocrites a final warning.
rows.anchor: an ultimatum is sounded to the Quraysh and the Hypocrites are given a final warning.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qur’an Group 1 primarily addresses the People of the Book and only secondarily Quraysh; Group 2 reverses that order.
rows.anchor: Group 1 of the Qur’ ān is directed to the People of the Book. If the Quraysh are addressed, it is only in a secondary way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Group 2 argues mainly from human nature, intellect, and the world, whereas Group 1 uses matters the People of the Book acknowledged.
rows.anchor: In Group 2, arguments are mostly drawn from the signs found in human nature and intellect and in the world around human beings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Group 1 believers replace the People of the Book as religious leaders; in Group 2 they replace Quraysh as custodians of the House.
rows.anchor: In Group 1, the People of the Book are deposed from religious leadership and their place has been given to the believers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah invites Quraysh to monotheism, the hereafter, and Muhammad’s prophethood, warning them with the fate of nations that rejected messengers and using Abraham’s argument to identify his true followers.
rows.anchor: They are invited to profess faith while arguments in favour of monotheism, the hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening points to self-evident signs for monotheism and the hereafter and marvels at Quraysh’s aversion to them.
rows.anchor: Some obvious arguments in favour of monotheism and the hereafter are pointed to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rejecting the Qur’an amounts to rejecting truth, with consequences; what it foretells is destined to occur.
rows.anchor: Denying the Qur’ ān is tantamount to denying the truth which will have its consequences.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah recalls that God punished those who rejected messengers and alludes to early Arab history.
rows.anchor: Those who deny God’s Messengers were divinely punished. Early history of the Arabs is referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even the greatest requested miracle would not convince the rejecters.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is assured that the greatest of miracles will not be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier messengers were mocked, and their mockers ultimately received the punishment they had ridiculed; Muhammad is directed to recall this history to Quraysh.
rows.anchor: Ultimately, they were inflicted with the very punishment they had made fun of.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since everything belongs to God and He has made mercy incumbent upon Himself, a Day of Judgment must come.
rows.anchor: He has made mercy mandatory upon Himself. Hence it is essential that He bring about a Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet disavows polytheism; good and evil remain in God’s hands, and all are subject to His wise, knowing power.
rows.anchor: Good and evil are in the hands of God. Everyone and everything is subservient to His power.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God supplies decisive evidence for monotheism, the Qur’an carries it, and true People of the Book recognize it; only the unfortunate remain deprived.
rows.anchor: The decisive evidence for monotheism and polytheism is from God and He bears witness in favour of the former.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Polytheists falsely ascribe partners to God and will be stunned, unable to answer when asked about them at Judgment.
rows.anchor: they would be asked about the partners they associated with God, they will be taken aback and will have no answer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some hear the call only to rebut it foolishly and dismiss Qur’anic accounts as tales instead of learning from them.
rows.anchor: it is not to understand and accept it; it is merely to counter it with foolish arguments.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When they see Hell they will regret their wretchedness and wish to return to worldly life; at Judgment they lament having wasted it.
rows.anchor: Their eyes will only open when they will stand near Hell. At that time, they will express regret and sorrow on their wretchedness

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their present assumption that worldly life is all there is will collapse when they face their Lord.
rows.anchor: Today they think that the life of this world is all that there is.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should not grieve over ridicule for refusing to produce a punishment sign: the mockery is really directed at God, so he should leave the matter to Him.
rows.anchor: They are not making fun of him; they are actually making fun of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier prophets also endured such circumstances patiently, and God’s help eventually came according to His unchanging practice.
rows.anchor: This is God’s established practice and it never changes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only people capable of recognizing truth will believe; dead hearts reject even the greatest signs, and the world's signs cannot benefit the blind.
rows.anchor: God’s heavens and earth are replete with signs but what can they avail the blind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier peoples demanded signs, but calamities only hardened their hearts further before God uprooted them.
rows.anchor: God inflicted them with various calamities. However, instead of becoming attentive towards God, their hearts hardened even more.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier peoples who hardened themselves after calamities were ultimately uprooted by God.
rows.anchor: were uprooted by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad claims neither divine treasures nor unseen knowledge; he follows only what God reveals.
rows.anchor: He only follows what is revealed to him from God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should warn those who fear God and the hereafter, ignore demands for miracles, and welcome poor believers seeking God’s pleasure without turning them away to attract arrogant elites.
rows.anchor: As for those who seek God’s pleasure and want to listen to his message, he must not distance them from himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet rejects polytheism and religious innovation on clear revealed evidence; only God can send punishment, whose time is appointed.
rows.anchor: He can send His torment whenever He intends from where He desires. Every event has an appointed time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God controls every person’s life and can send punishment from wherever and whenever He wills.
rows.anchor: The life of every person is in God’s hands.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every event has an appointed time, and the disbelievers will soon know it.
rows.anchor: Every event has an appointed time. These disbelievers will soon know.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When hostility prevents listening, the Prophet should avoid debate and leave them to themselves; his task is reminder, not forcing faith.
rows.anchor: his task is to just to remind and advise them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After truth and guidance arrive, only their wretchedness can make them stray; the Prophet and companions will follow God’s specified path.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) and his companions will tread the same path as has been specified by God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage invokes Abraham’s argument for monotheism against his people.
rows.anchor: The argument in favour of monotheism communicated by Abraham (sws) to his nation is referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets before and after Abraham are briefly recalled, and Muhammad is urged to adhere firmly to the guidance they taught.
rows.anchor: The real guidance is the one these prophets have pointed to. The Prophet (sws) should strongly adhere to it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Monotheism is argued from signs in the world surrounding human beings.
rows.anchor: Arguments of monotheism drawn from the world around human beings are presented.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage refutes polytheism and makes each person responsible for choosing error after guidance has arrived.
rows.anchor: once guidance has come to them, he who still chooses the path of error will himself be responsible for it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers must follow revelation and ignore idolaters, and must not insult their idols lest they retaliate by insulting God.
rows.anchor: without any justification they must not disgrace the idols and deities of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers’ oath to believe if shown a miracle is rejected: once people have failed to believe, even every kind of sign will not change them.
rows.anchor: if they are shown all kinds of miracles, even then those who have by that time have not accepted faith will never do so.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God allows human and jinn devils to lure people when messengers call, exposing those who choose evil; the Prophet must hold to God’s Book.
rows.anchor: the devils among the jinn and humankind are also given an opportunity to lure them to evil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers should resist polytheistic dietary innovations and may consume what Abraham’s religion and the Qur’an have not forbidden; the Prophet should disregard those stumbling in disbelief.
rows.anchor: They can freely consume things which were neither forbidden in the religion of Abraham (sws) nor has the Qur’ ān proscribed them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophethood is granted by God, who alone knows who is worthy; arrogant claims to worldly and otherworldly success invite punishment, while faith depends on God’s governed urge and grace.
rows.anchor: Only God knows who is worthy of it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deviant jinn and humans will admit their wrongdoing despite conclusive proof; Quraysh still have time to reform before the promised punishment.
rows.anchor: they reached this fate because of their misdoings even after the truth had been conclusively conveyed to them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rejects idolaters’ superstitions that prohibit certain crops and animals and sacrifice human beings to idols.
rows.anchor: they would forbid certain crops and animals to themselves and would sacrifice human beings to please their idols.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Debate should concern Muhammad’s actual invitation, not claims he never made about treasures, the unseen, or angelhood; he follows revelation.
rows.anchor: Why do they dispute with him regarding things he never has laid claim to?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blind and sighted image distinguishes those who follow desire from those who discern truth; since righteous and wrongdoers cannot share a fate, refusal to show a demanded punishment sign does not undo reward and punishment.
rows.anchor: Will the righteous and the wrongdoers have the same fate? If the answer to this question is in the negative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This section tells Muhammad to leave sign-demanders, warn those fearing God and the hereafter, and preserve access for poor believers rather than appease arrogant elites.
rows.anchor: those who were demanding signs and punishments. However, he should warn through this book those who fear God and the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believers seeking religious understanding are worthy of the Prophet’s attention, while the poor’s presence is itself a trial for wealthy opponents.
rows.anchor: Nor should he turn away the poor among the believers merely to please these arrogant elements.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is not accountable for arrogant people’s refusal, and neither are they accountable for his duties in a way that could justify his turning believers away; doing so would be injustice.
rows.anchor: Similarly, these people will not be held responsible on the Day of Judgement for the duties imposed on him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wealth, status, and lineage obstruct the elites’ faith: they assume a religion cannot be entrusted to people who are poor and socially low.
rows.anchor: the wealth, status and lineage of these arrogant people have become a barrier for them against accepting faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God grants worldly goods to worthy and unworthy alike but gives the treasure of religion only to the grateful.
rows.anchor: God gives the treasures and pleasures of this world to both the worthy and the unworthy

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poor believers receive special affection, and every element of God’s greeting and blessing conveys success in both worlds.
rows.anchor: every word of the salutations and blessings they receive from God carries glad tidings of success in both worlds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an should warn people who fear being gathered before God without a guardian or intercessor; they can benefit and reform, whereas those with no afterlife fear or trust in intercessors will not believe despite signs.
rows.anchor: those who use their intellect and insight and who fear that they will be one day gathered before their Lord

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an itself is the most natural and logical instrument of warning, rather than punishment signs.
rows.anchor: the most natural and logical means for warning is the Qur’ ān and not signs of punishment.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an benefits only those whose natural faculties remain alive.
rows.anchor: This Qur’ān will also benefit only those whose natural abilities are alive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An erroneous belief in intercession is the greatest obstacle to piety and charity.
rows.anchor: the greatest impediment to piety and charity is the erroneous concept of intercession.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad must not abandon sincere worshippers to appease wealthy, arrogant people who disparage his poor companions.
rows.anchor: he should not waste any more time on the wretched among them who are inebriated by their status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh leaders disparaged the companions as poor menial workers and argued that respectable people could not join a religion that welcomed them; Muhammad must not lose true companions to win these elites.
rows.anchor: his companions were all poor who did menial jobs and how could God select such lowly sections of the society for His religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the elites persist in error, they alone bear its consequence; turning away genuine seekers would leave the Prophet liable for neglecting those deserving his care.
rows.anchor: If he goes after these wretched elements, they will not be held responsible on his behalf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Addressing Muhammad rather than the Quraysh directly strikes at their arrogance and implies they are unworthy of direct address.
rows.anchor: instead of addressing them, the Prophet (sws) is addressed. This is to make evident to them that they are not even worthy of being addressed directly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb used for driving the poor away is harsh and means to disregard someone disparagingly, matching what Quraysh wanted Muhammad to do to his companions.
rows.anchor: it means to disparagingly disregard someone.

rows.speaker: Jesus (sws)
rows.claim: Jesus’ lost-sheep parable depicts a shepherd seeking one straying sheep instead of being content with the ninety-nine.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) has stated a parable also: “What do you think? If a man owns a hundred sheep

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lost-sheep parable illustrates God’s affection for people who return after error and a prophet’s concern for his nation’s faith.
rows.anchor: Just as this parable shows the great affection God has for people who turn to Him after being in error

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophetic concern for people reflects God’s affection and is praiseworthy, but it has limits: the Prophet must not pursue the wayward at the expense of loyal companions.
rows.anchor: God does not want his prophet to go after those people who have gone astray at the expense of his real companions.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Farāhī discusses important points on this topic in his commentary on Sūrah ‘Abas; Islahi says he will give his own view later.
rows.anchor: Ustādh Far āhī has written some very important points related to this topic in his exegesis of Sūrah ‘Abas.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In liyaqūlu, the lām marks consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), not causation.
rows.anchor: the particle لis for ‘āqibah that expresses the consequence and it is not causative.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s wealth and poverty are tests rather than proof that recipients deserve their circumstances.
rows.anchor: if some people are given wealth by Him in this world, it is not because they deserve it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Affluence tests gratitude and humility rather than arrogance; poverty tests patience, contentment, and acceptance rather than resentment toward God.
rows.anchor: It is a heavenly favour and divine mercy which is specific for only those who were grateful to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religious favour is not a visible luxury that can be displayed as social status; it is divine mercy given to the grateful.
rows.anchor: God’s religion is not gold, silver, silk or velvet whose saddles or pieces of cloth can be seen on donkeys

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ingrates who use God’s inward and outward favours against Him have no share in the favour of religion.
rows.anchor: As for the wretched and ingrates who used all the inner and outer favours God blessed them with against God Himself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s religion is a heavenly mercy reserved for the grateful who use their faculties and avoid arrogance; worldly pleasures, unlike religion, reach both good and wicked people.
rows.anchor: Worldly pleasures are received by both the good and the wicked. However, the gift of religion is only given to those who are grateful to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Salām can be used when meeting, parting, or welcoming someone.
rows.anchor: it is also used at the times of welcoming someone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels welcome steadfast monotheists to Paradise with a greeting of peace.
rows.anchor: angels while welcoming those who had remained steadfast on the belief of monotheism will say

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad’s welcoming greeting reverses the Quraysh chiefs’ demand that he distance himself from poor believers.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is directed to adopt an attitude opposite to what the chiefs of the Quraysh demanded

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poor believers seek only their Creator’s pleasure, so the promised mercy and forgiveness answer their actual desire rather than worldly status or riches.
rows.anchor: The only desire they had was to please their creator and master.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These believers do not value what worldly people passionately seek, in this life or the next.
rows.anchor: there is no weight in the eyes of the believers of things which these slaves of the world vehemently desire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause coordinated with “so that the path of criminals becomes clear” is elided; repeating that phrase restores the sense, which summarizes believers’ and disbelievers’ attitudes to reassure the Prophet.
rows.anchor: If it is unfolded, the verse would read:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet rejects worship of partners and religious innovations because God has forbidden them on clear evidence; revelation testifies for him, while punishment is God’s exclusive prerogative.
rows.anchor: It is in fact God’s prerogative only.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dead will be raised and gathered before the same God for accountability, a reality witnessed in daily life but missed by those who shut their eyes.
rows.anchor: after they die, people will be raised to life one day and after that all will be gathered before the same God and held accountable.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In distress people call on God alone but return to foolish ways when delivered; the punishment demanded by Muhammad’s opponents will arrive at its appointed time.
rows.anchor: as soon as they are delivered by Him from this trial they immediately return to their previous foolish ways
